stem: Which file scopes an MCP server to a single project?

options.label: A
options.body: `.mcp.json` (in the repo).
options.rationale: Correct. Project scope is `.mcp.json` in the repository; user scope is `~/.claude.json`.

options.label: B
options.body: `~/.claude.json`.
options.rationale: That's user scope — it applies across all your projects, not to a single one.

options.label: C
options.body: `.claude/settings.json`.
options.rationale: Not the MCP server config file; MCP project scope is `.mcp.json`.

options.label: D
options.body: `mcp.config.yaml`.
options.rationale: Not a real MCP configuration file.

stem: Your team shares a `.mcp.json` in the repo, but each developer also runs a personal analytics MCP server only they use. Teammates keep accidentally committing their personal server into the shared file. What's the right fix?

options.label: A
options.body: Move personal servers to user scope (`~/.claude.json`); keep only shared servers in `.mcp.json`.
options.rationale: Correct. User-scope config is per-developer and lives outside the repo, so personal servers can't be committed to the shared project file.

options.label: B
options.body: Add the personal server to `.mcp.json` and `.gitignore` that file.
options.rationale: Gitignoring the shared file breaks it for everyone — the team servers need to be committed.

options.label: C
options.body: Put the personal server in a root CLAUDE.md so it's documented.
options.rationale: CLAUDE.md is for conventions/instructions, not MCP server configuration.

options.label: D
options.body: Have each developer comment out their personal server before committing.
options.rationale: Relies on human discipline every commit — exactly the failure happening now. Scope separation fixes it structurally.

stem: Per the guide, what are the four MCP error categories used in a structured error response?

options.label: A
options.body: transient, validation, business, permission.
options.rationale: Correct. Those are the four categories, carried alongside the isError flag, an isRetryable boolean, and a human-readable description.

options.label: B
options.body: fatal, warning, info, debug.
options.rationale: Those are log severity levels, not the MCP error categories.

options.label: C
options.body: network, timeout, auth, unknown.
options.rationale: Plausible-sounding but not the guide's categories (transient/validation/business/permission).

options.label: D
options.body: client, server, gateway, retry.
options.rationale: Not the MCP error categories.

stem: One agent is configured with 18 tools and frequently picks the wrong one or ignores the right one. What's the most effective structural fix?

options.label: A
options.body: Distribute the tools across specialized agents so each has a focused set (roughly 4–5), rather than 18 on one.
options.rationale: Correct. Too many tools dilutes selection; the guide's example is 18 instead of 4–5. Splitting tools across agents by role restores reliable selection.

options.label: B
options.body: Set tool_choice to "any" so the model always calls some tool.
options.rationale: "any" forces a tool call but doesn't help it pick the right one — and can cause loops.

options.label: C
options.body: Force a specific tool with tool_choice {"type":"tool","name":...} for every request.
options.rationale: Forcing one tool removes the model's judgment entirely; it's not a general fix for tool overload.

options.label: D
options.body: Add few-shot examples of each of the 18 tools.
options.rationale: Doesn't address the core problem — 18 tools on one agent still dilutes attention regardless of examples.

stem: Two tools, `search_orders` and `find_order`, have nearly identical descriptions, and the agent keeps calling the wrong one. What's the most effective fix?

options.label: A
options.body: Rewrite the descriptions to state each tool's distinct purpose, inputs, and boundaries (when to use it and when not to).
options.rationale: Correct. The model selects tools from their descriptions; clear, non-overlapping descriptions with explicit boundaries are what make selection reliable.

options.label: B
options.body: Merge them into one tool that does both.
options.rationale: Sometimes reasonable, but if the two serve genuinely different needs, merging loses that; the immediate defect is ambiguous descriptions.

options.label: C
options.body: Rename them to tool_a and tool_b.
options.rationale: Opaque names make selection worse — the description is what guides the model.

options.label: D
options.body: Lower the temperature so tool choice is deterministic.
options.rationale: Determinism just makes the wrong-tool choice consistent; it doesn't clarify which tool to use.

stem: An automated code-review agent flags far too many false positives, eroding developer trust. What's the most effective first improvement?

options.label: A
options.body: Give the prompt explicit criteria for what counts as a reportable issue (and what to ignore).
options.rationale: Correct. Explicit, precise criteria raise precision and cut false positives directly — the standard first move before heavier machinery.

options.label: B
options.body: Switch to a more capable model tier.
options.rationale: Costly and doesn't tell the model your bar for what's worth flagging.

options.label: C
options.body: Post every finding but sort by a confidence score.
options.rationale: Still floods reviewers with noise; the goal is to not raise the false positives in the first place.

options.label: D
options.body: Run the review only on changed lines.
options.rationale: Narrows scope but doesn't fix the criteria producing false positives within that scope.

stem: A `skills: string[]` extraction is inconsistent: compound phrases like "Python and SQL" are sometimes split and sometimes not, implied skills appear, and array lengths vary wildly. The prompt says "Extract all skills mentioned." Best fix?

options.label: A
options.body: Add few-shot examples demonstrating compound-phrase splitting, explicit-mention criteria, and appropriate granularity.
options.rationale: Correct. All three issues are about how the model interprets "a skill." Concrete examples teach the pattern — split vs. not, mentioned vs. inferred, right granularity.

options.label: B
options.body: Constrain it: "Extract 10–20 skills max, one per entry, only explicitly named."
options.rationale: Hard count caps are arbitrary and force the model to drop real skills or invent filler to hit the range.

options.label: C
options.body: Add post-extraction normalization to a canonical taxonomy and dedupe.
options.rationale: Post-processing can't fix inferred-but-unstated skills or decide how to split "Python and SQL" — that's an extraction-time decision.

options.label: D
options.body: Enrich the schema to {skill, confidence, source_quote}[].
options.rationale: Useful metadata, but it doesn't resolve the underlying inconsistency in how skills are parsed.

stem: A validation-retry loop appends the specific error and re-sends on failure, fixing most issues in 2–3 attempts. For which failure is additional retrying LEAST effective?

options.label: A
options.body: The model outputs "et al." for co-authors when the full list exists only in an external document not in the input.
options.rationale: Correct. Retry-with-feedback only fixes mistakes the model could have gotten right from the source. If the information isn't in the input, no amount of retrying supplies it.

options.label: B
options.body: Keywords come back as a nested object when the schema requires a flat string array.
options.rationale: A structural mismatch the model can correct once told the expected shape.

options.label: C
options.body: Citation counts arrive as locale strings ("1,234") when integers are required.
options.rationale: The value is present; the model just needs to stop formatting it — easy for feedback-retry.

options.label: D
options.body: Dates come back as full ISO datetimes when only YYYY-MM-DD is required.
options.rationale: Pure formatting fix — the underlying value is correct and can be trimmed on retry.

stem: Which statement about the Message Batches API is correct?

options.label: A
options.body: It offers ~50% cost savings with an up-to-24-hour processing window and uses custom_id to correlate results.
options.rationale: Correct. 50% savings, up to a 24-hour window, custom_id for correlation — and no multi-turn tool calling.

options.label: B
options.body: It guarantees results within 5 minutes.
options.rationale: There's no fast-latency SLA; the window is up to 24 hours.

options.label: C
options.body: It supports multi-turn tool calling like the real-time API.
options.rationale: Batch does not support multi-turn tool calling.

options.label: D
options.body: It costs the same as the Messages API but runs asynchronously.
options.rationale: It's ~50% cheaper — that's the point of using it for latency-tolerant work.

stem: Code generated in a session passes that same session's self-review, but an independent reviewer finds three security gaps. Why does self-review miss them, and what's the fix?

options.label: A
options.body: The generating session retains its own reasoning/justification, biasing it against questioning its decisions — use a separate (multi-instance) review pass with fresh context.
options.rationale: Correct. Same-session review carries the rationale that led to the code, so it's less likely to challenge it. A fresh, independent instance reviews without that bias.

options.label: B
options.body: The generation session used a weaker model than review.
options.rationale: Same model — the issue is context bias, not capability.

options.label: C
options.body: Claude can't review code it generated due to a technical limitation.
options.rationale: There's no such limitation; self-review works but is biased.

options.label: D
options.body: The self-review prompt just needs more detail.
options.rationale: More detail doesn't remove the reasoning-context bias of the same session.

stem: During multi-step identity verification, after the customer answers the third question the agent asks for their name again, as if the earlier exchange never happened. Most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.body: The conversation history isn't being included in subsequent API requests.
options.rationale: Correct. The API is stateless — each request must include the full messages array. Send only the latest turn and the model has no memory of earlier ones, producing exactly this 'ask again' symptom.

options.label: B
options.body: The verification tool clears the agent's internal state after each step.
options.rationale: Tools don't clear agent state; conversation state lives in the messages you send.

options.label: C
options.body: The prompt lacks an instruction telling Claude to remember across turns.
options.rationale: Memory across turns comes from passing prior turns into the request, not from an instruction.

options.label: D
options.body: Claude's memory is limited to two turns by default and must be configured to extend.
options.rationale: No such default limit exists; history length is under your control, bounded by the context window.

stem: In a coordinator + subagents pipeline, a document-analysis subagent times out mid-task. How should the failure propagate so the system stays reliable and debuggable?

options.label: A
options.body: The subagent returns a structured error (what failed, which task, retryable?) to the coordinator, which decides whether to retry, reassign, or continue with partial results.
options.rationale: Correct. Structured error propagation to the hub keeps the coordinator in control and observable — it can retry, reroute, or degrade gracefully with the rest of the findings.

options.label: B
options.body: The subagent silently returns empty output so the pipeline keeps moving.
options.rationale: Silent empties look like 'no data found' and corrupt downstream synthesis — the failure is hidden.

options.label: C
options.body: The subagent crashes the whole pipeline so nothing proceeds on incomplete data.
options.rationale: Total failure throws away all the other subagents' valid work; graceful degradation is better.

options.label: D
options.body: The subagent retries indefinitely on its own until it succeeds.
options.rationale: Unbounded self-retry hides the problem from the coordinator and can hang the pipeline.

stem: 12% of extractions contain semantic errors that pass schema validation. Reviewers can only check 20% of outputs. How should you allocate their attention?

options.label: A
options.body: Have the model emit field-level confidence scores, calibrate a threshold on a labeled set, and route the low-confidence slice to reviewers.
options.rationale: Correct. Field-level confidence concentrates the 12% errors into the low-confidence slice; routing that 20% catches far more errors than random sampling.

options.label: B
options.body: Randomly sample 20% of extractions for review.
options.rationale: Great for measurement, poor for coverage — random catches only ~20% of the 12% (~2.4%).

options.label: C
options.body: Review only extractions with empty required fields.
options.rationale: The 12% problem is wrong values in populated fields, which an empty-field filter misses.

options.label: D
options.body: Review only documents with unusual formatting.
options.rationale: Formatting anomaly doesn't reliably predict where fields got confused.
